name: Real World Evidence and AI
blurb: Using AI to turn health records and claims into regulatory evidence.
title: Real World Evidence and AI
answer: Real world data from health records, claims, registries and wearables can support regulatory decisions, and AI is used to extract clinical concepts from unstructured records. In one study natural language processing identified key clinical concepts with 94.1 percent accuracy against 49.0 percent for traditional methods.

reading.body:
Natural language processing extracted key clinical concepts from health records at 94.1 percent accuracy, against 49.0 percent for traditional methods.

That gap is the whole argument for using AI on real world data. Health records, claims, registries and wearables hold the material regulators will accept as real world evidence, but the clinical concepts inside them sit in unstructured text that older extraction methods read poorly. A method that finds the right concept roughly half the time cannot carry a regulatory submission. One that finds it nearly always can, which is why the FDA framework for real world evidence matters here: it defines what such data must show to support a decision, and extraction quality is what determines whether the data clears that bar.

The constraint is not the model alone. Records and claims are large, longitudinal, and held by institutions that must permit their use, so the compute and governance sit with the data holders as much as with the AI. The 94.1 percent figure comes from one study, so it describes a demonstrated result rather than a settled standard, and it does not establish how that accuracy holds across different record systems, coding practices, or patient populations.

If AI derived variables feed regulatory evidence, the extraction model itself needs the credibility evidence the framework asks for. The data here does not say what that validation requires, or how long it takes.

explainer:
Real world data are health data collected outside trials: electronic health records, insurance claims, registries, and data from wearables and apps. Real world evidence is what analysis of those data shows about a medicine's use, benefits or risks. Regulators increasingly accept it for some purposes, such as supporting new indications, external comparators and safety monitoring, when the data are fit for purpose and the methods sound.

Much of the most useful information sits in free text, such as notes describing symptoms, disease progression or reasons for stopping treatment. AI, especially natural language processing, extracts these details at scale, turning narrative records into analysable variables. The catch is that the extraction becomes part of the evidence: if a model decides which patients had a given outcome, its accuracy affects the result, so it must be validated and documented like any other method.

What real world evidence is

Real world evidence is what can be learned about a medicine from data collected outside controlled trials: health records, insurance claims, registries, pharmacy data, devices worn by patients, and patient reported outcomes. Regulators accept it for some decisions, including safety monitoring after approval, support for new indications in some circumstances, and external comparators for trials in rare diseases where a control group is impractical. The evidence is only as good as the data and the methods, which is where most of the scrutiny falls.

What AI does with it

Machine learning turns unstructured records, such as clinical notes, imaging reports and pathology, into structured variables that analyses can use; this is the step that most limited real world evidence before. Models also find comparable patients across datasets, estimate treatment effects while adjusting for the differences between patients who received different treatments, detect safety signals and predict outcomes. Each of these is an active research area, and regulators have published guidance on what they expect from the data, the study design and the transparency of methods.

Where the caution lies

Patients in the real world are not randomised, so differences in outcomes can come from differences in who got the drug rather than from the drug. AI does not solve that; it can make it worse by finding patterns that are artefacts of how care is recorded. Regulators therefore expect pre registered protocols, documented data provenance, validation of any AI derived variables against expert review, and sensitivity analyses. Used within those expectations, AI has made real world evidence faster to produce and broader in scope, and it has become routine in post approval safety work.
